{{Short description|Probabilistic concept}}

In [[mathematics]], more specifically in stochastics, '''Doob's h-transform''' is a method to transform a [[Markov process]] into a new Markov process, which exhibits certain properties. Most prominently, for a homogeneous Markov process <math>X</math> with (random) lifetime <math>T</math>, the reverse process <math>(X_{T-t})_{t\geq 0}</math> and the conditioned process <math>X\mid X_T=x</math> on terminating at a single point <math>x</math>, can be expressed as an <math>h</math>-transform of the original process via some deterministic function <math>h</math>. The method was first introduced by [[Joseph L. Doob|J. L. Doob]] in 1957 to analyze quotients <math>f/h</math> of [[Subharmonic function|superharmonic]] functions <math>f</math> and (positive) [[Harmonic function|harmonic]] functions <math>h</math> from a probabilistic point of view.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Doob |first=Joseph L. |authorlink=Joseph L. Doob |date=1957 |title=Conditional Brownian motion and the boundary limits of harmonic functions |journal=Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France |volume=45 |pages=431–458 |doi=10.24033/bsmf.1494 |doi-access=free |hdl=2027/mdp.39015095252097 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Doob |first=Joseph L. |authorlink=Joseph L. Doob |date=1958 |title=Probability and the first boundary value problem |journal=[[Illinois Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=2 |pages=19–36 |doi=10.1215/ijm/1255380830 |doi-access=free }}</ref>{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=334}}

The key advantage of Doob's <math>h</math>-transform is that the transition probabilities of the transformed process are explicitly given as functions of <math>h</math>. If <math>X</math> is an [[Itô diffusion]], for example a [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]], then under relatively mild conditions, the <math>h</math>-transformed process is again an Itô diffusion with an explicit drift term depending on <math>\nabla\log h</math>.{{sfn|Särkkä|Solin|2019|pp=113–115}}

== Motivation ==
Consider a <math>d</math>-dimensional [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]] <math>W</math> started in <math>x_0</math> and stopped at the time <math>T</math>, when it first hits the unit ball <math>B</math>, and one is interested in the process <math>W^x</math> of <math>W</math> conditioned on hitting some point <math>x\in\partial B</math> at time <math>T</math>. In law, <math>W^x</math> is given by<math display="block">\mathbb P^{x_0}(W^x\in A) := \mathbb P^{x_0}(W\in A\mid W_T=x)=\mathbb P(W\in A\mid W_T=x,W_0=x_0),</math>for any Borel set <math>A\subset \{f\in C([0,\infty),\R^d):f(0)=x_0 \}</math>.

According to [[Bayes' theorem|Bayes formula]], for some fixed <math>t\geq 0</math>, conditioning <math>W_t</math> on <math>W_T</math> can be expressed in terms of the distribution of <math>W_T</math> given <math>W_t</math> and the distribution of <math>W_t</math>, namely for <math>M\in\mathcal B(\R^d)</math><math display="block">\mathbb P^{x_0}(W_t\in M\mid W_T=x)= \frac{1}{q(x\mid x_0)}\int_M q(x\mid y) \mathbb P^{x_0}(W_t\in\mathrm{dy}),</math>with<math display="block">q(x\mid y):= \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb P(W_T\in\cdot\mid W_t=y)}{\mathrm{d}\sigma}(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb P^y(W_T\in\cdot)}{\mathrm{d}\sigma}(x),</math>where <math>\sigma</math> denotes the uniform distribution on the sphere. In this context, the function <math>q</math> happens to be the well-known [[Poisson kernel]], which has the explicit formula<math display="block">q(x\mid y)=\frac{1}{\sigma(\partial B)}\frac{1-\lVert y\rVert^2}{\lVert x-y \rVert^d}, \qquad x\in\partial B,\,y\in B.</math>The distribution of <math>W_t</math> under <math>\mathbb P^{x_0}</math> is explicit as well, since the Brownian Motion is a [[Gaussian process]] and so the Bayes formula for <math>W^x_t</math> gives an explicit way to compute the transition probabilities. The Bayes formula from above is precisely an <math>h</math>-transform of <math>W</math> with <math>h=q(x\mid\cdot)</math>.

For the simulation of <math>W^x</math>, one is interested in a [[stochastic differential equation]] for the latter. With the Bayes formula from above, the [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] <math>\mathcal A^x</math> of <math>W^x</math> can be related to the generator <math>\mathcal A=\frac{1}{2}\Delta</math> (the [[Laplace operator]]) of Brownian motion: For <math>f\in C^2(\R^d)</math>, and by denoting the [[Feller process|Feller semigroups]] of <math>W</math> and <math>W^x</math> by <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> and <math>(P_t^x)_{t\geq 0}</math> respectively, it holds for <math>y\in\R^d</math>{{sfn|Rogers|Williams|2000|p=83–86}}<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathcal A^x f(y)&=\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{P_t^xf(y)-f(y)}{t} \\
&= \frac{1}{q(x\mid y)}\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{P_t(q(x\mid\cdot) f)(y) - q(x\mid y)f(y)}{t} \\
&= \frac{1}{q(x\mid y)}\mathcal A(q(x\mid\cdot)f)(y)\\
&=\frac{1}{q(x\mid y)}\nabla_y q(x\mid y)\cdot \nabla f(y) +\frac{1}{2}\Delta f(y),
\end{align}</math>because <math>\Delta q(x\mid\cdot)=0</math>. Comparing <math>\mathcal A^x</math> with the generator of a general [[Itô diffusion#The generator|Itô diffusion]], one can conclude that<math display="block">\mathrm{d}W^x_t = \nabla\log q(x\mid W_t) \, \mathrm{d}t + \mathrm{d}W_t, \qquad W_0=x_0.</math>

== Definition ==

=== Homogeneous Markov processes ===
Let <math>X</math> be a homogeneous [[Markov chain|Markov process]] with state space <math>E</math>, which is often assumed to be a [[Locally compact space|locally compact]] [[Polish space]] to guarantee the existence of [[Regular conditional probability|regular conditional expectations]], and denote its transition semigroup by <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math>. Let <math>h:E\to[0,\infty]</math> be an ''excessive'' function, that is,{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=45}}<math display="block">\begin{align}
\forall t\geq 0:&\int_E h(y) P_t(x,\mathrm{d}y)\leq h(x),\\
\lim_{t\to0} &\int_E h(y) P_t(x,\mathrm{d}y)= h(x).
\end{align}</math>Then the <math>h</math>-transform <math>X^h</math> is defined as the Markov process with transition semigroup <math>(P_t^h)_{t\geq 0}</math> defined by<math display="block">P_t^h(x,A):= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{h(x)}\int_A h(y)P_t(x,\mathrm{d}y), &x\in E\smallsetminus \{h=0 \text{ or } h=\infty\} \\
0, &x\in \{h=0 \text{ or } h=\infty\}
\end{cases}</math>for all <math>t\geq 0</math> and <math>A\in\mathcal B(E)</math>.

This definition implies that in general <math>P_t^h(x,E)\leq 1</math>, which means that the process need not staying inside its state space for all times. For such processes, one usually defines an additional ''cemetery state'' <math>\partial\notin E</math> that the process enters with probability <math>1-P_t(x,E)</math> for all <math>x\in E</math> and which it never leaves again, i.e., <math>P_t(\partial,\{\partial\})=1</math>. In other words, the process is allowed to be ''killed'' at some finite time. On the extended state space <math>E_\partial=E\cup\{\partial\}</math>, the <math>P_t^h(x,\cdot)</math> with the previous definitions are probability measures for all <math>x\in E_\partial</math> by construction.

The points <math>x\in\{h=0 \text{ or } h=\infty\}</math> are so-called ''branching points'', for which it holds <math>P_0(x,\{x\})=0</math> and <math>P_0(x,\{\partial\})=1</math>. Thus, the <math>h</math>-transformed process never enters the set <math>\{h=0 \text{ or } h=\infty\}</math>, and it is killed at the random time <math>T^h=\inf\{t\geq 0: X_t^h=\partial\}</math>.

=== Inhomogeneous Markov processes ===
Let <math>X</math> be an inhomogeneous [[Markov chain|Markov process]] with values in <math>\R^d</math>, inhomogeneous transition probabilities <math>(P_{t,s})_{t\geq s\geq0}</math> and let <math>h:[0,\infty)\times\R^d\to(0,\infty)</math> be ''space-time regular'', that is, for <math>s>0</math>, <math>t\geq 0</math> and <math>x\in\R^d</math>{{sfn|Särkkä|Solin|2019|pp=113–115}}{{sfn|Rogers|Williams|2000|p=83–86}}<math display="block">h(t,x)=\int_{\R^d} h(t+s,y) P_{t+s,s}(x,\mathrm{d}y).</math>Then the <math>h</math>-transform <math>X^h</math> is defined as the (inhomogeneous) Markov process with transition probabilities <math>(P_{t,s}^h)_{t\geq s\geq0}</math> defined by<math display="block">P_{t+s,s}^h(x,A):= \frac{1}{h(t,x)}\int_A h(t+s,y)P_{t+s,s}(x,\mathrm{d}y),\quad \forall x\in E, A\in\mathcal B(E).</math>

== Properties ==
In the theory of <math>h</math>-transforms for homogeneous Markov processes <math>X</math> on a filtered probability space <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\geq0},\mathbb{P})</math> it is assumed that{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=320}}

# <math>X_0</math> is distributed according to some distribution <math>\mu</math>,
# <math>X</math> has a ''lifetime'' <math>T</math>, that is, a [[random variable]] (not necessarily a [[stopping time]]) such that <math>X_t(\omega)\in E</math> for <math>t>T(\omega)</math> and <math>X_t(\omega)=\partial</math> for <math>t\geq T(\omega)</math>,
# <math>X</math> is a strong Markov process with [[càdlàg]] paths on <math>(0,T)</math>.
For simplicity, the underlying probability space is usually chosen as the canonical space of càdlàg paths with values in <math>(E,\mathcal B(E))</math> and <math>X</math> as the identity.

=== Probabilities ===
The transition semigroup <math>(P^h_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> generates a family of probability measures <math>(\mathbb{P}_h^x)_{x\in E}</math> on the canonical space of càdlàg paths. For any stopping time <math>\tau</math>, it holds for <math>A\in\mathcal F_\tau</math> and <math>x\in E\smallsetminus\{h=0\text{ or }h=\infty\}</math>{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=325}}

<math display="block">\mathbb{P}_h^x(A,T>\tau)=\frac{1}{h(x)}\mathbb{E}^x[1_A h(X_\tau)].</math>

For a family <math>(u_s)_{s\in S}</math> of excessive functions on <math>E</math> over an index set <math>S</math> (and measurable w.r.t. the product <math>\sigma</math>-algebra on <math>E\times S</math>), if <math>h</math> is of the form

<math display="block">h(x)= \int_S u_s(x) \, \mathrm{d}\beta(s)</math>

with some finite measure <math>\beta</math> on <math>S</math>, then for <math>A\in\mathcal F</math> the probability simplifies to{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=326}}

<math display="block">\mathbb{P}_h^x(A)=\frac{1}{h(x)}\int_S u_s(x) \mathbb{P}_{u_s}^x(A) \, \mathrm{d}\beta(s).</math>

=== Infinitesimal generator ===
As an almost direct consequence of the above, if <math>X</math> has infinite lifetime (<math>T=\infty</math>) and has generator <math>A</math>, then the generator of its <math>h</math>-transformed process <math>X^h</math> is

<math>\begin{align}
A^hf(x)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\mathbb E^x[f(X_t^h)]-f(x)}{t}
&= \frac{1}{h(x)}\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\mathbb E^x[f(X_t)h(X_t)]-f(x)h(x)}{t} \\
&=\frac{1}{h(x)}A(fh)(x)
\end{align}</math>

for all <math>x\in E</math> and all functions <math>f</math> such that <math>fh</math> is in the domain of <math>A</math>.

=== Killing ===
If <math>\tau</math> is a ''co-optional time'', that is, if for any <math>t\geq 0</math> it holds <math>\tau\circ\theta_t=(\tau-t)^+</math>, where <math>(\theta_s)_{s\geq 0}</math> is the [[Markov property#Alternative formulations|shift-semigroup]], then one can define<math display="block">\begin{align}
&h(x):= \mathbb P^x(\tau>0), \quad x\in E\\
&X_t^\tau:=\begin{cases}
X_t, &t<\tau \\
\partial,& t\geq\tau
\end{cases}
\end{align}</math>for which it holds that <math>X^\tau</math> is an <math>h</math>-transform of <math>X</math>.{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=331}}

=== Time-reversal ===
The time-reversal <math>\overleftarrow{X}</math> of <math>X</math> is defined as

<math display="block">\overleftarrow{X_t}(\omega) = \begin{cases}
X_{T(\omega)-t}, & t\leq T(\omega)\\
\partial, & t> T(\omega) \text{ or } T(\omega)=\infty 
\end{cases}.</math>

<math>\overleftarrow{X}</math> is again a homogeneous Markov process, however now with left-continuous paths.{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|pp=303–304}}

If <math>X^h</math> has initial measure <math>\nu \propto h\cdot\mathrm{d}\mu</math>, then the reverses of <math>X</math> and <math>X^h</math> have the same transition probabilities. In particular, for a co-optional time <math>\tau</math> (for example a last hitting time), if <math>X</math> starts in a fixed point [[almost surely]], then the reverses of <math>X</math> and <math>X^\tau</math> have the same transition probabilities.{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=333}}

Moreover, if <math>X</math> possesses a dual process <math>\hat X</math> (defined below), then its reverse can be expressed as an <math>h</math>-transform of its dual. To formulate this statement, we define for <math>X</math> and <math>\hat X</math> respectively the transition semigroups <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> and <math>(\hat{P}_t)_{t\geq 0}</math>, and, for <math>p\geq 0</math>, the ''resolvents''

<math display="block">\begin{align}
U_p := \int_0^\infty e^{-pt} P_t \, \mathrm{d}t, \\
\hat{U}_p := \int_0^\infty e^{-pt} \hat{P}_t \, \mathrm{d}t.
\end{align}</math>

While for <math>p>0</math> the resolvents are always finite, <math>U_0</math> can become infinite.

As the dual of <math>X</math>, <math>\hat X</math> must fulfill for some measure <math>\nu</math>

# <math>\hat X</math> is a strong Markov process with càdlàg paths,
# For all <math>p\geq0</math> and <math>f,g\geq0</math> measurable: <math>\int_E \int_E f(y)U_p(x,\mathrm{d}y)g(x) \, \mathrm{d}\nu(x) = \int_E f(x)\int_E g(y)\hat{U}_p(x,\mathrm{d}y) \, \mathrm{d}\nu(x),</math>
# For all <math>p\geq0</math> and <math>x\in E</math>, both <math>U_p(x,\cdot)</math> and <math>\hat{U}_p(x,\cdot)</math> are absolutely continuous w.r.t. <math>\nu</math>.
By setting

<math display="block">h(y) := \int_E \frac{\mathrm{d}U_0(x,\cdot)}{\mathrm{d}\nu}(y) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x):=\int_E u_0(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x),\quad y\in E,</math>

if <math>0<h<\infty</math>, then <math>\overleftarrow{X}</math> and <math>\hat{X}^h</math> have the same transition probabilities.{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=366}}

=== Conditioning ===
Doob's <math>h</math>-transform can also be used to condition the process <math>X</math> on hitting a distinct point or, more generally, to attain a pre-determined distribution at its lifetime. For simplicity, it is supposed that <math>\hat P_0(x,\{x\})=1</math> for all <math>x\in E</math>, that is, the dual process <math>\hat X</math> has no branching points.

Let <math>y\in E</math> and <math>U_0</math> be the resolvent of <math>X</math> for <math>p=0</math> as defined above. Then with

<math display="block">h(x)=u_0(x,y),</math>

it holds that <math>X^h_{T-}=\lim_{t\uparrow T}X_t^h=y</math> almost surely on <math>\{T<\infty\}</math>.{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=368}}

If <math>\mu=\delta_{x_0}</math>, that is, <math>X</math> starts in <math>x_0</math> almost surely, and <math>\alpha</math> is a distribution on <math>E</math> such that

<math display="block">\beta(A) = \int_A\frac{1}{u_0(x,y)}\mathrm d \alpha(y), \quad A\in\mathcal B(E),</math>

is a <math>\sigma</math>-finite measure, then one can achieve <math>X^h_{T-}\sim \alpha</math> by choosing{{sfn|Chung|Walsh|2005|p=368}}

<math display="block">h(x):= \int_E u_0(x,y)\mathrm d\beta(y) = \int_E \frac{u_0(x,y)}{u_0(x_0,y)} \, \mathrm{d}\alpha(y).</math>

== Applications ==

=== Generative modelling ===
Doob's <math>h</math>-transform has begun to find applications in [[generative model]]ling, for example for point clouds, climate data, graphs and image segmentation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ye |first1=Mao |last2=Wu |first2=Lemeng |last3=Liu |first3=Qiang |date=2022 |title=First Hitting Diffusion Models for Generating Manifold, Graph and Categorical Data |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |volume=35 |arxiv=|pages=27280–27292 |doi=10.52202/068431-1978 |isbn=978-1-7138-7108-8}}</ref> The method has also been proposed for faster conditional training and sampling of [[diffusion model]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Denker |first1=Alexander |last2=Vargas |first2=Francisco |last3=Padhy |first3=Shreyas |last4=Didi |first4=Kieran |last5=Mathis |first5=Simon |last6=Dutordoir |first6=Vincent |last7=Barbano |first7=Riccardo |last8=Mathieu |first8=Emile |last9=Komorowska |first9=Urszula Julia |last10=Lio |first10=Pietro |date=2024 |title=DEFT: Efficient Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models byLearning the Generalised h-transform |journal=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |volume=37|pages=19636–19682 |doi=10.52202/079017-0620 |isbn=979-8-3313-1438-5}}</ref>
